newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela and ANC chiefs meet in bush to talk jobs.
newsitem.headline: Mandela and ANC chiefs meet in bush to talk jobs.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela and his top ANC colleagues locked themselves in a secret South African bush hideaway on Thursday to plan government and party policy over the next two years, his last in power.

Sources in the ruling African National Congress said making the labour market more flexible, which the ANC's union allies fiercely resist, will be high on the agenda along with job creation in general.
"If that is the case, it is a very encouraging sign," BOE Natwest economist Nick Barnardt told Reuters.
"What's decided at this meeting will set the tone for the next six months on market reforms," he said. "This is probably the most important single meeting of this year."
ANC spokesman Ronnie Mamoepa said the four-day closed-door "bush council", at an undisclosed rural venue near Johannesburg, would "chart the way forward for the next two years".

All 55 members of the party's National Executive Committee, provincial and other ANC leaders are attending the session which will start with a keynote speech by Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, almost certain to succeed Mandela as president in 1999.
Mandela will address its close on Sunday.

Economists said that deregulating the job market, a stated goal of the government's macro-economic plan which Finance Minister Trevor Manuel unveiled in June, was the toughest task this year facing South Africa, where one in three is jobless.

They said the markets also wanted to see an acceleration of other economic policy reforms outlined in that plan, such as cuts in the fiscal deficit, privatisation and the relaxation of foreign exchange controls.

The economic plan, a far cry from the socialist goals the ANC sought before it came to power in the first all-race elections in 1994, aims to double growth to six percent and create 400,000 jobs annually by 2000.
While loathe to see cut-rate wages in a country just coming out of decades of racial exploitation, the government says some labour deregulation is vital, but has given no clear details.

Collective bargaining, working hours, job security and union representation are areas which could be looked at. But the ANC faces strong opposition from its two formal allies, the powerful Confederation of South African Trade Unions and the communists.
Financial markets are watching to see whether the government will press ahead, prevaricate damagingly or yield to its partners' pressure and row back from the economic plan.

Barnardt said he was in no doubt that the ANC's bush council would determine in part the line for Manuel's eagerly awaited presentations to South African financial institutions next month and for the annual budget, due on March 12.
The ANC's Mamoepa said a whole range of topics would be discussed at the meeting, with details released only afterwards.
"It will develop a comprehensive two-year government and organisational programme of action to accelerate South Africa's process of transformation and development," he said.
